doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Identifying 'Dynamic Duo' and its bass-and-piano arrangement
summary: He names his tune 'Dynamic Duo' and explains why the bass and piano solo first, inspired by a late-sixties gig with Chambers and Harris.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You were indicating finding your audience for young musicians and reaching them. I want you to see if you can name this tune. Are you ready?
Okay. Well I know what it is already but go ahead. I think it’s mine — I think it’s an intro.
to a tune I wrote for my last CD and last record project, and it’s entitled “Dynamic Duo.”
Yeah. And it features David Wong, bassist and Jeb Patton, pianist. And both of whom were with my group.
I want to ask you about the, not just the writing of it but the arrangement. Way back in ’98 when we spoke you said, “The writing process is the loneliest, most miserable thing.”
Oh for me — I’m sure it is not with everybody but, yeah.

But beyond the initial tune I found that the arrangement of it was compelling because you had that very memorable little lick and then it went into this unison piano and bass complex, followed by a bass solo, and it wasn’t until over like 3-1/2 minutes that we heard anything as far as a sax or trumpet solo.
Was this a conscious decision to —

Yeah. It was. Yeah. Because most of the time you’re going to get the trumpet or the saxophone or the horns play first. So just for the sake of variation and, you know, to add a different flavor, you know I like to have the bass or piano player play first, not only in clubs but on records as well. And it was written to be their feature you know. It was written to be their feature. And it was basically inspired by my involvement with Paul Chambers, Barry Harris, Billy Higgins, and Lonnie Hillyer, a trumpet player, and myself. We had a gig and you know the great Barry Harris and also Paul Chambers both Detroit people, and of course I’m from Detroit and Lonnie Hillyer, the trumpet player was from Detroit as well. So Billy Higgins who is I think from California or Texas or something like that. But that was the rhythm section of a gig many years ago, in the late sixties. And so I was kind of inspired by the way Paul Chambers and Barry Harris played with each other. So fast forward to now, when we decided to do a record, a live record date with Smoke Records in New York, I wanted — that CD and record project is dedicated, it’s a tribute to Barry Harris, a great pianist and my mentor as a kid. And so I really wanted to just my tipping of the hat to Paul Chambers and Barry Harris. Because during that gig these two people, and Billy Higgins, I mean these people were really playing really well with each — really good with each other you know. And it was inspiring to hear that. And I just said let me write something for this great bass player of today, which is David Wong, and great young pianist Jeb Patton, and just write a really interesting tune, or figure for bass and piano.
